I need to write unit tests for DefaultInjectionEngine without mocking capabilities since Mockito isn't available in the classpath—only powermock-reflect, cglib, objenesis, and similar libraries. I'm checking through the available jars to see what testing tools I actually have to work with.

This is the Defects4J Mockito-28b scenario, meaning the Mockito source code itself (Reporter, MockitoException, FieldInitializer, MockCandidateFilter) is compiled directly into the project's classpath rather than being an external jar dependency. So I can import these classes directly and test with real field instances and real objects instead of mocks, since there's no mocking framework available to create test doubles.

I'm tracing through injectMocksOnFields: it loops through each @InjectMocks annotated field, copies the mocks set, and calls FieldInitializer to initialize the field using either a default or argument constructor.

When a MockitoException gets caught during initialization, it calls Reporter().cannotInitializeForInjectMocksAnnotation() but never rethrows or assigns the result, so execution continues with the field instance still null. Then when the code tries to call getClass() on that null instance, it triggers a NullPointerException -- this looks like the known defects4j Mockito-28b bug where the exception handling fails silently and leads to an NPE downstream.

Right, cannotInitializeForInjectMocksAnnotation throws a MockitoException when invoked, so the call should terminate execution there rather than falling through to the getClass() line. That confirms the real bug: field initialization failure should properly throw instead of letting null propagate to the NPE site.

Now I'm thinking through test coverage needed: a normal case injecting mocks into various field types, a failure case expecting MockitoException for fields that can't be instantiated, type-based matching with multiple mocks, name-based disambiguation, and inheritance hierarchies where fields exist across subclass and superclass.

I should also cover edge cases like empty injectMocksFields sets, empty mocks sets, setter vs field injection, and multiple @InjectMocks fields. Since only the public injectMocksOnFields method is accessible and internal filters aren't exposed, I need to rely on that API and confirm the target class can be imported correctly from the available classpath.

Since this is a defects4j scenario, the full Mockito source should already be compiled on the test classpath, so I can freely reference org.mockito.* internals as part of the same codebase. I'll design simple test fixture classes: a base service and subclass, plus tested objects with fields that either have no setter (for field injection) or have a setter (for setter injection), to validate both injection paths.

I also want superclass/subclass field hierarchies to test inherited field injection, and an interface-typed field to trigger instantiation failure since interfaces can't be instantiated by the field initializer. I'll structure these as static nested helper classes inside the test file for simplicity.

Now I'm planning the actual test methods: starting with an empty fields set that should do nothing, then building out cases for successful injection scenarios.

Test 2 checks that when mocks are empty, a field remains null after injection is attempted. Test 3 verifies simple type-based injection assigns a matching mock. Test 4 confirms setter injection takes priority over field injection when both are available on the target object.

I'm adding a setterCalled flag to the test class so I can confirm the setter was actually invoked rather than the field being set directly. Test 5 checks that fields across a class hierarchy, both superclass and subclass, get properly injected with their respective mocks.

Test 6 handles ambiguity: when two mocks of the same type exist and neither matches the field name, the injection algorithm should bail out and leave the field null rather than guessing.

Since these mocks aren't created via actual Mockito.mock() calls, checking the mock name against the field name could throw an exception rather than fail gracefully. Given this uncertainty, it's safer to avoid asserting on this ambiguous-mocks scenario unless I can verify the exact source behavior, rather than guessing at internal filter logic that isn't documented.

For the field-initialization-failure test, I'm considering an interface field that can't be instantiated via a no-arg constructor, which should trigger FieldInitializer to throw a MockitoException internally that gets caught and rethrown through the reporter's cannotInitializeForInjectMocksAnnotation() path - I need to confirm this chain actually holds before asserting it in the test.

Next I want a test covering multiple @InjectMocks fields across different holder classes, using a container with two distinct fields to confirm both get processed. I'll extract the fields via reflection and mark them accessible before running the initializer.

I should also verify FieldInitializer's behavior for interfaces or abstract types—since it relies on finding an accessible constructor to lazily instantiate the field, it will throw a MockitoException if no concrete constructor exists.

Now I'm sketching out the full test class, planning imports for JUnit assertions, reflection utilities, and Mockito's internal injection engine, while sticking with plain JUnit assertions since AssertJ and Hamcrest are optional dependencies.

I'm setting up the nested helper classes: a ServiceA base class and ServiceB subclass, plus FieldOwner classes with and without setters to test field injection behavior.

I'm also sketching SuperOwner/SubOwner hierarchies with protected service fields, and a holder with an interface field since interfaces can't be instantiated directly. Now I'm reasoning through how injectMocksOnFields works—the Field objects represent annotated fields on the test class instance, so I need to trace carefully how reflection pulls those fields for injection.

I'm building a container class with a single FieldOwner field, then grabbing that field via reflection to pass into the injection call, so I can later verify the field gets correctly populated.

For the other test cases, I'll extend this pattern: containers with a setter-based field, a subclassed owner for hierarchy testing, containers with two different field types for the multi-field test, and a case with an ambiguous field name matching a specific mock when multiple same-type mocks exist.

I'm now considering the ambiguous-mocks test more carefully - using plain ServiceA objects instead of real Mockito mocks could cause NameBasedCandidateFilter to throw when trying to extract a mock name, since MockUtil may reject non-mocks. Based on the javadoc's "don't fail" philosophy, I'd expect ambiguous matches to simply leave the field unset rather than throw, but I'm uncertain whether the filter's mock-name lookup is safe for non-mock objects.

Given the uncertainty, I'll keep that ambiguous-mocks test lenient, only asserting no exception is thrown, with a TODO noting the uncertain internal filtering. For solid coverage I'll add a separate unambiguous test using two mocks of distinct types (SubOwner/SuperOwner) matching two different fields precisely, which better validates the typical branch than guessing at exact resolution behavior.

Now I'm turning to the "cannot initialize field" branch, using a container class with an interface-typed field (like Runnable). I set up the field set, an empty or irrelevant mocks set, and a test instance, expecting that calling injectMocksOnFields throws a MockitoException since interfaces can't be instantiated via FieldInitializer -- verifying this with @Test(expected = MockitoException.class) while double-checking that FieldInitializer's fallback logic actually triggers that exception for interface types with no existing instance.

Beyond that, I need a test for multiple @InjectMocks fields being processed independently in the outer loop, and a test proving mocks aren't consumed globally—since the mocks set is freshly copied per field, two separate fields requiring the same mock type should both receive the same mock instance rather than one "stealing" it from the other.

I also need tests for mismatched-type mocks leaving fields null without exceptions, verification that field injection works via reflection when no setter exists on FieldOwner, and a setter-preferred test case using a class with both field and setter.

I'm also planning a dedicated test for the supertypesLast comparator's effect: a single class declaring two related-type fields (ServiceA and ServiceB extends ServiceA), to confirm injection order respects specificity when both fields live in the same class rather than a hierarchy.

If subtype fields process first, the mock gets consumed by fieldSubType, leaving fieldSuperType null—confirming sub-type-before-super-type ordering. So I'm testing a class declaring the supertype field first and subtype field second, then verifying the comparator still sorts the subtype field ahead for processing since ServiceA.isAssignableFrom(ServiceB) returns true, forcing the supertype field later in ascending order.

I'll provide a single mock instance of ServiceB, expecting it to be injected into the subtype field while the supertype field stays null, which indirectly validates the comparator's branch logic. I'll need reflection with setAccessible to pull field values back since the fields are protected and the test lives in a different class.

I'm assembling the full test file now, including a helper method to retrieve field values via reflection, and making sure to call setAccessible(true) on any Field objects I build before passing them into the injection set, defensively mirroring Mockito's typical internal behavior.

Now I'm listing out the full set of test cases I need to cover: null injectMocksFields, null mocks set, empty cases, single matching mock injection via field access, setter preferred over field injection, and more scenarios covering multiple mocks and edge cases.

Rounding out the list, I add tests for class hierarchy injection across subclass and superclass, ensuring mocks aren't consumed twice, supertype ordering priority, multiple injectMocks fields each getting their own mock copy, instantiation failures throwing MockitoException, and ambiguous multiple candidates of the same type being handled leniently without exceptions.

Now I'm working through the null-pointer edge cases: when injectMocksFields is null, the for-each loop throws NPE immediately, and when mocks is null, I need at least one valid field in injectMocksFields so the loop body executes and hits the NPE when constructing the HashSet from mocks. For the case of an empty injectMocksFields set with non-null mocks, I'm checking that the loop simply doesn't execute and no exception occurs.

For the fourth test case with one field but an empty mocks set, I expect the FieldInitializer to instantiate the field normally via its default constructor but leave the inner service field null since there's nothing to inject, with no exception thrown either.

Now I'm writing the final test class, double-checking the imports for MockitoException and DefaultInjectionEngine match the correct package paths, and planning to define the helper classes as private static nested classes inside the test file so everything stays self-contained with accessible default constructors.

setAccessible should override access checks regardless of package, consistent with Mockito's typical internal behavior, so I'll note that as an assumption and move on to writing the full file. For the ambiguous multiple-candidates test, I'm considering whether using plain non-Mockito-mock objects as candidates could cause issues if the name-based filter internally calls MockUtil.getMockName, since that method might behave differently or throw when given a non-proxy object rather than an actual mock created via Mockito.mock().

Actually, the javadoc is explicit here: when ambiguous between candidates, it says "don't fail, user will then provide dependencies" — meaning no exception, field stays unset. I'll trust that documented behavior and assert the field remains null with no exception thrown, since the underlying mock-checking internals aren't visible to reason about further.

For the interface field test case expecting a MockitoException on instantiation failure, I need to reconsider whether FieldInitializer wraps such failures in its own exception type that still qualifies as a MockitoException subtype.

Since the source catches MockitoException specifically, that confirms FieldInitializer must throw that exception type when initialization fails. But whether Reporter().cannotInitializeForInjectMocksAnnotation actually propagates an exception upward, or just logs and returns silently leaving the field instance null, isn't clear from what I can see — if it's the latter, subsequent code trying to access that null instance would fail differently.

Actually, I recall now - the real Mockito-28 bug was that the method returned a MockitoException instead of throwing it, so the call site created the exception object but never threw it, leaving the injected field null and causing a NullPointerException on the next line instead of the intended error.

This confirms Test 12 should expect a NullPointerException, not a MockitoException, since that's the actual observable fault.

This confirms the mechanism: Reporter likely returns the exception rather than throwing it directly, which is exactly why the downstream NPE occurs when the injected field stays null.
